statedGuarantee: A four-layer defense-in-depth containment architecture for a production fleet of nine autonomous OpenClaw agents handling PHI: (L1) gVisor kernel-level workload isolation on Kubernetes so that a manipulated agent's execution blast radius is confined to the sandbox; (L2) a credential proxy sidecar so the agent container never possesses raw API secrets; (L3) per-pod Kubernetes NetworkPolicy egress allowlists restricting each agent to named destinations; (L4) an application-layer prompt integrity framework (framework-injected trusted metadata envelopes, explicit untrusted-content labeling, five AGENTS.md anti-injection rules) intended to blunt identity spoofing and indirect prompt injection. The composed claim is that the infrastructure layers hold regardless of whether the LLM complies with its instructions, so that the documented agentic failure modes do not become HIPAA-reportable PHI disclosures.
advertisedRhetoric: "Caging the Agents"; "a four layer defense in depth approach"; "kernel level workload isolation using gVisor sandboxed containers on Kubernetes"; "infrastructure level controls (kernel isolation, credential proxy, network egress) that operate independently of the LLM's compliance with instructions"; and for Layer 4 "a prompt integrity framework with cryptographically structured metadata envelopes" - T1-flavored language that Section 4.4.1 never cashes out (no signature, MAC or key is described; the envelope is merely "injected by the framework, not by user input").
tierSpan: gVisor implements a user space kernel (Sentry) that intercepts all system calls from the containerized agent, filtering and mediating access to host resources.
cheapestDefeat: No kernel escape is needed. Working the tier explicitly: the guarantee is that a manipulated agent cannot escape the sandbox, cannot hold raw secrets, and cannot reach a destination outside its per-pod allowlist. The mechanisms that must fail are the gVisor Sentry syscall boundary and the CNI-enforced NetworkPolicy - both bind the process regardless of intent, so the floor is T2, not T3. The cheapest adversary action is an over-broad capability, which the T2 definition explicitly admits as a T2 defeat: every agent class carries at least one general-purpose, write-capable destination on its allowlist (api.anthropic.com for all agents; api.github.com and api.linear.app for R&D agents; hooks.slack.com and api.telegram.org for operations agents), so an agent compromised through injected content exfiltrates PHI through a permitted destination without violating any policy. The paper widens this itself by conceding that domain allowlists resolve to rotating CDN and load-balancer IPs, so the enforced IP set is coarser than the intended domain set. Two further cheap defeats: (a) the GCP metadata endpoint is itself allowlisted for the audit agent, a credential-minting channel the sidecar does not front; (b) for the fleet as actually run during the 90 days, Table 3 places gVisor, the proxy sidecar and NetworkPolicy in the unshipped "K8s Target" column, so on the measured system the cheapest defeat was reading a world-readable openclaw.json (mode 664 and 644) from any local process - a T2 misconfiguration defeat.
placementSpan: agent corruption via indirect prompt injection through external editable resources

coverageSpans.E1: The agent cannot access other containers’ file systems, escalate privileges to the host, or pivot to adjacent infrastructure.
coverageSpans.E2: Even if an agent is manipulated (through prompt injection or non owner compliance) to execute malicious shell commands, the blast radius is contained to the sandboxed environment.
coverageSpans.E3: Implementation challenges include DNS resolution for allowlisted domains (CDN and load balancer IP rotation requires periodic policy updates or DNS aware policy controllers) and exception management when agents need temporary access to new destinations during development.
coverageSpans.E4: The proxy enforces request level policies: rate limiting, destination allowlisting, and payload size limits.
coverageSpans.E5: Agents have unrestricted shell access, file system access, package installation capabilities, and the ability to communicate via messaging platforms and email.
coverageSpans.E6: Security audit agents: all fleet VM IPs, GCP metadata endpoint, api.anthropic.com
coverageSpans.E7: The positive behavior documented in CS#9 (collaborative troubleshooting between agents) is preserved by the architecture; the security controls do not prevent beneficial inter agent communication.

schneider.surrogate: Three monitorable safety properties, each enforced by a mechanism outside the model: no syscall from the agent or any descendant reaches the host kernel except through the gVisor Sentry; no packet leaves the agent pod for an address outside its NetworkPolicy allowlist; and no raw API secret exists inside the agent container (secrets live only in the sidecar, held as Kubernetes Secrets under RBAC). A fourth, weaker surrogate is the continuous fleet audit: no credential file on any fleet VM has permissions looser than 600 and no credential is exported in a shell rc file.
schneider.objective: An information-flow hyperproperty plus an intent property, neither of which a reference monitor can enforce: that Protected Health Information never flows from an agent to an unauthorized party (HIPAA 164.312(e) transmission security, 164.404 breach avoidance), and that the agent acts only on instructions from its legitimate owner rather than on injected or spoofed ones. Non-exfiltration is a non-interference property over pairs of executions, so no single-execution monitor can decide it - and every listed allowlist contains a destination through which PHI can lawfully leave. The paper is unusually candid about the gap at Layer 4, conceding that prompt injection is a structural feature of LLM-based systems and that the prompt integrity framework "cannot provide the same level of assurance as the infrastructure layers," positioning the surrogates as blast-radius reduction rather than as enforcement of the objective.

notes:
CHARITABLE READING APPLIED, AND WHERE IT COST SOMETHING.

1. DEPLOYMENT STATUS is the single most important thing an adjudicator must know. The abstract says the architecture was "developed and deployed" for nine production agents, but Section 6.4 calls the Kubernetes four-layer stack "The current migration target," and Table 3 places gVisor sandboxing, the credential proxy sidecar, NetworkPolicy egress and the full prompt integrity framework in a column headed "K8s Target" - i.e. not shipped. What actually ran for the 90 days is the VM progression: Gen 1 unhardened, Gen 2 UFW deny-all plus fail2ban plus chmod 600, Gen 3 iptables outbound logging plus VPC Flow Logs plus Cloudflare Gateway DNS filtering plus AGENTS.md anti-injection rules. DNS filtering is a T3 chokepoint defeated by dialing an IP directly. I scored the architecture as designed (T2) per the charitable stance; a strict coder would score the deployed system T3 and would be right on the record. This is the paper's largest gap between rhetoric and artifact.

2. "Cryptographically structured metadata envelopes" (abstract, repeated in 4.4.1) is T1 rhetoric with no T1 mechanism behind it. Section 4.4.1 describes the envelope as a schema (openclaw.inbound_meta.v1) "injected by the framework, not by user input" that "The LLM is instructed to trust." No signature, MAC, key or verifier appears anywhere in the paper. This is the coding instructions' worked example in the wild: even a genuinely signed envelope whose only enforcement is an in-context instruction to the model scores T3, because the binding is the model's willingness to honor a label, not a verification step. I credited T1 nowhere.

3. E1 and E2 marked covered on the strength of the syscall-interception claim: gVisor intercepts ALL system calls, and descendants spawned inside the sandbox face the same Sentry, so the E2 depth rule is satisfied by construction rather than by enumeration. Note carefully what is and is not guaranteed: this is CONTAINMENT, not AUTHORIZATION. Inside the cage the agent retains unrestricted shell, can rewrite its own AGENTS.md, SOUL.md and IDENTITY.md (Section 2.1: every configuration file "can be modified by the agent itself"), and can spawn whatever it likes. No file write or subprocess spawn is ever approved, denied or logged per-action; only the boundary is enforced. If the SoK's covered/partial distinction tracks mediation-against-a-policy rather than mere confinement, E1 and E2 should drop to partial. That is my main coding judgment call and I flag it for adjudication.

4. E3 partial, not covered, on the paper's own concession about CDN and load-balancer IP rotation (the covert-channel rule applies: an honest, documented gap is still a gap), and because every listed allowlist contains a general-purpose write-capable destination. The pod-level NetworkPolicy does reach descendant egress, which is why this is partial rather than worse.

5. E4 partial: git push is possible only via api.github.com (allowlisted for R&D agents) using a PAT the agent never holds, so the credentialed path is genuinely chokepointed by sidecar plus egress policy. But no repository, branch or content policy is described, the sidecar is specified for HTTP APIs (Anthropic is the worked example) with no mention of git-over-SSH, and a push to an attacker-readable repo is itself an exfiltration channel that both L2 and L3 permit.

6. E5 partial: package install is named only as a hazardous capability (Section 2.1), never as a defended effector. Coverage is incidental - gVisor contains install-hook execution and the pod NetworkPolicy bounds hook egress - so both halves of the E5 depth rule are formally reached, but the network half inherits E3's weakness and no registry pinning, SBOM, provenance or install-hook policy appears anywhere in the paper.

7. E6 partial, and the credential list is the reason. Section 4.2 enumerates what the sidecar holds ("Anthropic API keys, GitHub PATs, Linear tokens, GCP service account keys"), which is close to a published list, but two things contradict full coverage: the GCP metadata endpoint sits explicitly on the audit agent's egress allowlist, and instance-metadata credential minting is a credential channel the sidecar does not front; and findings M1 through M4 (scattered workspace .env files, and a workspace .env containing tokens) are recorded as Open, not Remediated, in Table 2 at publication.

8. E7 partial: sub-agent spawn is listed as a first-class agent capability in the introduction, and the architecture deliberately declines to mediate agent-to-agent interaction - Section 7 preserves CS#9 cross-agent collaboration as "Positive behavior (no defense needed)." In-pod sub-processes inherit L1 containment and the egress allowlists do bound which agents most classes can reach, but only the privileged audit agent is granted "all fleet VM IPs," and the paper's own CS#10 scenario has a corrupted agent attempting to shut down other agents. No authorization decision is ever made about spawning or delegating to another agent.

9. ADVERSARY PLACEMENT. Primary A2: the entire six-domain threat model is built on untrusted inbound content - non-owner instructions over messaging and email, spoofed display names, and malicious instructions injected via an externally editable GitHub Gist linked from an agent's memory file. Secondary A3, because the paper explicitly treats the agent's own operating instructions as attacker-writable and argues the infrastructure layers hold "independently of the LLM's compliance with instructions." Secondary A4, because Section 8.2 names the audit agent Tony "the highest value target in the fleet," holding SSH to all nine VMs - an insider-in-the-orchestrator placement the design addresses (scoped service account, immutable audit logs) but never tests. Secondary A1, because the credential findings mean any local process or network caller reaching a VM could read every secret the agent possessed. A5 is not addressed beyond trusting gVisor and GCP.

10. EVIDENCE GRADE L1, and here is the tension. What is behaviorally confirmed is the AUDIT system and hygiene remediation: four HIGH findings discovered and fixed the day of discovery with "post remediation verification confirmed clean state," plus measured gVisor overhead (2-5 ms on TCP setup, 20-40 percent on sequential reads). What is NOT confirmed is the containment architecture itself. Table 4 maps all eleven Shapira et al. case studies to defense layers, but no attack from that corpus was ever executed against this architecture - the mapping is analytic, not empirical. The one efficacy claim for Layer 4 ("untrusted content labeling reduces compliance with injected instructions in our testing") carries no numbers, no method and no sample. Open-sourced Helm charts and NetworkPolicy templates make source inspection possible, which is why I graded L1 rather than L0. A coder who counts the same-day remediation verification as behavioral evidence of a control could argue L2 for the credential-hygiene subset alone.

11. WHY IT EARNS ITS PLACE IN THE CORPUS: it is one of the few entries that composes across tiers on a named production fleet rather than proposing a single mechanism - OS isolation, credential compartmentalization, network policy and prompt-layer labeling - with the author correctly ranking Layer 4 as "the most brittle of the four defense layers" and stating that the purpose of the infrastructure layers is to survive its failure. That layered-honesty framing, plus the audit-agent-paradox discussion in 8.2, is the reusable contribution. The unreusable part is the headline claim of coverage across nine of eleven attack patterns, which is a mapping exercise rather than a result.

12. PROVENANCE: the empirical foundation is Shapira et al., "Agents of chaos," arXiv:2602.20021, whose eleven case studies supply nearly every threat scenario. Author states affiliations VP of Trust, Commure and Founder and CEO, nFactor Technologies. The fleet, the findings and the VM names are self-disclosed about the author's own deployment (Appendix A: "The vulnerabilities documented in this paper were found in our own production deployment, not in commercial products.").
